title: Advanced Autonomy — Learning Contracts

pts: A learning contract is a formal, negotiated agreement specifying a learner's goals, methods, timeline and self-assessment criteria.
This extends Unit 48's goal-setting work into a genuinely formalised, documented structure.
The contract's negotiated nature — not simply teacher-assigned — is central to its autonomy-building function.
points.who: Malcolm Knowles's andragogy and learning-contract framework

v: Learners’ goal sheets from earlier work (Unit 48); a contract template

items: Ask learners to take out their earlier goal sheets and read their goals aloud to a partner.
Show a four-column contract template: Goal, Methods and resources, Evidence, How it will be judged, plus a timeline row and signature lines.
In pairs, learners decide which of their goals could become a six-week contract goal and which are too vague as they stand.
Each learner drafts one row of the contract for a single goal.
Explain that the draft is the start of a negotiation: you will meet each learner to discuss and sign it.
Adults in a workplace course can link the contract to a real work outcome, such as writing a project report.
Support: provide a completed example contract to adapt.
Challenge: learners write contracts for two goals and justify the priority between them.

blocks.x: One row of a contract (written for this book):

lines: Goal: Follow English news discussions on television without subtitles by mid-March.
Methods and resources: Watch one 10-minute DD News or BBC segment three times a week; note five useful phrases each time.
Evidence: Listening log; a two-minute oral summary recorded in week 6.
How it will be judged: I summarize the main points and two supporting details; my teacher and I use the listening can-do descriptors.

blocks.x: A wish (‘improve my listening’) becomes a contract when it has a method, evidence and a criterion that someone else could check (Knowles 1986).

body: Purpose: to show how a vague goal is formalized. Content: a speech bubble ‘I want to get better at English’ passing through four labelled filters (goal, method, evidence, criterion) and emerging as a signed document. Style: clean, friendly diagram. Board version: four boxes in a row with arrows and a signature line.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared contract template that both learner and teacher can edit and comment on.

blocks.x: A printed or hand-copied contract glued into the back of each learner’s notebook.

pts: Goals in a learning contract should reflect genuine learner priorities, informed but not dictated by teacher expertise.
This connects to Unit 2's original needs analysis and Unit 47's motivation-reconnection work, now formalised into an explicit document.
A contract imposed rather than negotiated undermines the autonomy it's meant to build.

v: 5–7 minutes per learner over two weeks

items: Before the conference, reread the learner’s needs analysis and any earlier motivation notes (Unit 47).
Ask the learner to explain why this goal matters to them now.
Share any information the learner may lack, such as the demands of an upcoming exam or course.
Agree changes together; the learner writes the final wording.
Both sign and date the contract; each keeps a copy.
In a large class, hold conferences in groups of three learners with similar goals.
Support: offer a menu of three possible goals drawn from the needs analysis.
Challenge: learners propose their own success criteria before the teacher suggests any.

lines: T: You’ve chosen presentation skills. Tell me why.
S: Next year I have seminars in my B.Com course. I get very nervous.
T: That makes sense. The seminars will be about fifteen minutes. Is your goal about the language, the nerves, or both?
S: Both. But mainly I want to use signposting properly.
T: Good. Then let’s write the goal around signposting, and add rehearsal as a method for the nerves.

blocks.x: The teacher shares expertise but leaves the decision with the learner. A contract imposed rather than negotiated tends to become one more assignment, and the autonomy it was meant to build does not develop (Little 1991).

body: Purpose: to show negotiation as a two-way process. Content: two chairs facing each other, one labelled ‘learner priorities’, the other ‘teacher expertise’, with arrows meeting at a single signed goal between them. Style: warm, simple. Board version: two circles overlapping, with the goal written in the overlap.

items: Google Calendar or Microsoft Bookings (free with school accounts) for scheduling short conference slots.

blocks.x: A conference timetable written on the board and a tick list of learners seen.

pts: Have learners specify how they'll pursue each goal — which resources, which self-study strategies, on what schedule.
This connects to Unit 48's resource-evaluation skill, now applied to a learner's own concrete, committed plan.
The specificity here is what distinguishes a genuine contract from a vague aspiration.

v: Draft contracts; a list of resources evaluated earlier (Unit 48)

items: Show a vague methods column and a specific one side by side.
Learners underline every word in their own methods column that could not be checked.
For each underlined word, they answer: which resource, how often, for how long, and when?
Partners test each other’s plan with the question ‘Could I see you doing this?’
Learners revise and add a weekly schedule.
Learners build the schedule around real constraints, such as a long bus journey or a part-time job.
Support: provide a bank of resources grouped by skill and level.
Challenge: learners add a back-up plan for weeks when the main method is impossible.

lines: Vague: I will read more and learn new words.

Specific: On Monday, Wednesday and Friday, 7–7.30 a.m., I will read one chapter of a graded reader at level 5; I will record eight words with example sentences and a Telugu gloss in my vocabulary notebook, and review them on Sunday.

blocks.x: The second version can be checked, planned around and evaluated. Specificity is what separates a contract from an aspiration.

body: Purpose: to contrast vague and specific plans. Content: the same plan shown twice, once as out-of-focus text and once in sharp focus with times, resources and quantities highlighted. Style: photographic metaphor, simple. Board version: two columns headed ‘vague’ and ‘specific’.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a weekly study schedule with tick boxes.

blocks.x: A hand-drawn weekly grid in the notebook.

body: Ask learners to plan for less than they think they can do. A schedule of three realistic 30-minute sessions that actually happen is worth more than a daily plan abandoned in the second week.

pts: A self-access centre — physical or digital — provides curated resources organised for independent, self-directed use.
This gives learning contracts genuine infrastructure to draw on, rather than leaving resource-finding entirely to the learner.
Organisation by skill, level and goal type (not just alphabetically) makes a self-access centre genuinely usable.

v: Donated books, magazines, printed worksheets, a shelf or cupboard; QR codes for online material

items: Audit what the school already has: library books, old coursebooks, newspapers, graded readers, audio material.
Organize materials by skill (reading, listening, writing, speaking, vocabulary, grammar), then by level, then by goal type (for example ‘exam practice’ or ‘everyday conversation’).
Attach a simple card to each item: skill, level, time needed, and whether answer keys are available.
Add a signposting sheet: ‘If your goal is…, try…’.
Recruit learner helpers to maintain the collection and log what is borrowed.
Where space is short, build a ‘self-access box’ that travels between classrooms.
Not applicable (teacher and learner-helper activity).

blocks.x: Part of a signposting sheet (written for this book):

lines: Goal: understanding fast speech → Listening shelf, level B2: podcast transcripts with audio QR codes; news clips with gap-fill tasks.
Goal: formal letters and emails → Writing shelf: model texts with annotated structure (Unit 54); self-check lists.
Goal: academic vocabulary → Vocabulary box: word cards from the Academic Word List (Coxhead 2000).

blocks.x: Organization by skill, level and goal, not alphabetically, is what makes a collection usable for independent study (Gardner and Miller 1999).

body: Figure 56.4 A corner that points the way

Purpose: to show a self-access corner organized for use. Content: a small bookcase with shelves labelled by skill, coloured level stickers, a signposting poster above it and a borrowing log on a clipboard. Style: realistic, modest, clearly Indian school setting. Board version: a grid of skill columns and level rows.

items: Google Sites (free) or Padlet (free plan, limited number of boards) for a digital self-access collection.

blocks.x: A labelled cardboard box of photocopied materials with answer keys in an envelope.

pts: Periodic learner-advisor conferences review progress against the contract without reverting to teacher-directed instruction.
This connects to Unit 48's teacher-as-advisor role shift, now operating within a formal, scheduled structure.
The advisor's role is to ask good questions and offer resource suggestions, not to take back control of decisions.

v: 10 minutes per learner, every two to three weeks
The contract; the learner’s log or evidence

items: Ask the learner to bring the contract and log, and to say first how it is going.
Listen, then reflect back what you heard before offering anything.
Use open questions: What has worked? What got in the way? What will you change?
Offer resource suggestions only if the learner asks or seems stuck, and present them as options.
The learner writes any revision to the contract in their own words.
Pair teachers to observe each other’s advising sessions and count how many decisions were made by the learner.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Two responses to the same learner:

lines: S: I didn’t do the listening for two weeks. Exams in other subjects.
Directing: You must do it this week. Do three sessions.
Advising: That happens. Looking at the next three weeks, what would be realistic? Would a shorter session fit better?

blocks.x: Advisers use reflective dialogue, restating and open questions to help learners make their own decisions (Mynard and Carson 2012).

body: Purpose: to show advising moves. Content: a small toolbox holding cards labelled ‘listen’, ‘restate’, ‘ask’, ‘suggest options’ and ‘summarize’, with a crossed-out card labelled ‘decide for them’. Style: clean illustration. Board version: five words in a column with one struck through.

items: Google Forms (free) for a short pre-session check-in that learners complete before meeting.

blocks.x: A half-page advising record kept in a folder, one sheet per learner.

points.sub: Assessing the process, not just the outcome
pts: Assess both whether goals were achieved and how well the learner managed the autonomous process itself.
This distinguishes a learner who succeeded through good self-management from one who succeeded despite poor planning.
This connects to Unit 42's portfolio principle — the process of managing one's own learning is itself assessable evidence.

v: The contract; evidence produced; a two-part evaluation sheet

items: Learners assess the outcome: did they meet each goal against the criterion agreed at the start?
Learners then assess the process: planning, keeping to the schedule, adjusting when needed, and using advice.
Learners support each judgement with evidence from their log or portfolio (Unit 42).
Agree a final record that shows both parts separately.
Weight process and outcome equally, or let learners argue for a different weighting at the start.
Support: provide sentence starters (‘I kept to my plan when…’; ‘I changed my plan because…’).
Challenge: learners compare their self-evaluation with the teacher’s and explain any gap.

blocks.x: Two learners, same outcome (written for this book):

lines: Arjun met his goal, but his log shows nothing for four weeks and a rush in the last week. Outcome: met. Process: weak planning; did not adjust when behind.
Farah missed her goal by a small margin, but revised her plan twice after advising sessions and kept a full log. Outcome: nearly met. Process: strong self-management.

blocks.x: Assessing the process as well as the outcome recognizes that managing one’s own learning is itself a skill, and one that transfers beyond this contract (Zimmerman 2002).

body: Purpose: to show two dimensions of evaluation. Content: two parallel paths reaching the same flag; one is a straight, steady line with footprints, the other erratic with a sprint at the end. Style: simple, metaphorical. Board version: two lines to one flag.

items: Google Forms (free) for a structured self-evaluation.

blocks.x: A two-part evaluation sheet stapled to the contract.

pts: A learner struggling significantly with a learning contract may need to step back to a more structured, less autonomous approach temporarily.
This isn't a failure of the learner or the method — it's a signal that Unit 2's autonomy-readiness assessment needs revisiting.
Autonomy support should flex in both directions, not just toward ever-greater independence regardless of how it's going.

items: Identify learners whose logs show little activity or whose contracts have been revised repeatedly without progress.
In an advising session, ask how the contract feels and what kind of support would help.
Offer a more structured option, such as a teacher-set weekly task with one choice within it.
Present the change as a temporary adjustment, and agree when to review it.
Revisit the learner’s readiness for autonomy (Unit 2) and note what you have learned.
Offer a ‘buddy contract’, in which two learners share goals and check each other weekly.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s note (written for this book):

lines: Meena, week 4: log almost empty; says she ‘doesn’t know where to start’ each day. Agreed: for three weeks I set one reading task each week; she chooses the text from two options. Review in week 7.

blocks.x: Autonomy develops unevenly (Benson 2011). Support should flex in both directions, not only towards more independence.

body: Purpose: to show autonomy support as adjustable. Content: a dial labelled from ‘teacher-structured’ to ‘learner-directed’, with arrows showing it can turn both ways. Style: clear. Board version: a semicircle with a pointer and two arrows.

items: Google Sheets (free) to track contract activity and flag inactive learners.

blocks.x: A class list with a weekly tick for contract activity.

pts: A learning contract typically needs to fit within a broader scheme of work (Unit 14) and institutional assessment requirements.
Negotiate contracts within clearly stated boundaries — what's genuinely open to learner choice and what isn't.
This keeps autonomy-building realistic rather than promising a freedom the institutional context can't actually support.

v: 30 minutes to prepare; 15 minutes with learners

items: List what is fixed: the syllabus units, internal assessments and exam dates.
List what is open: choice of texts, topics, methods, pace and some evidence types.
Make a one-page ‘fixed and free’ chart and share it with learners before contracts are drafted.
Link contract goals to at least one scheme-of-work outcome so the work counts.
Negotiate with learners which of the ‘free’ elements they most want, and give extra time to those.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A ‘fixed and free’ chart for a first-year degree English course (written for this book):

lines: Fixed: the prescribed prose and poetry texts; two internal tests; the university examination format.
Free: choice of additional reading; personal vocabulary goals; the topic of one presentation; how to prepare for tests.
Linked: each contract goal names the course outcome it supports.

blocks.x: A contract that promises freedom the course cannot deliver damages trust.

body: Purpose: to show freedom within boundaries. Content: a garden with a clear fence labelled with fixed elements; inside, learners plant different crops labelled with their own goals. Style: warm, illustrative. Board version: a rectangle with ‘fixed’ written around the edge and learners’ goals inside.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable ‘fixed and free’ chart.

blocks.x: A chart-paper poster on the classroom wall.

body: With one B2 or C1 class, run a six-week pilot. Share a ‘fixed and free’ chart, negotiate one-goal contracts, hold one advising session midway and finish with a two-part evaluation. Note which learners flourished, which needed more structure, and what you will change next time.

dek: Unit 56 of 100: formalising self-directed learning for learners genuinely capable of it — structured enough to be accountable, open enough to remain their own.

aims.x: Unit 48 introduced learner autonomy as a set of habits built step by step: setting goals, choosing resources and reviewing progress. This unit takes the next step for learners who are ready for it. A learning contract turns those habits into a written, negotiated agreement that the learner owns, the teacher supports and the institution can recognize.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define a learning contract and explain what makes it different from an assigned task or a wish list;
negotiate goals with learners so that the contract reflects their priorities as well as your expertise;
help learners specify methods, resources and a schedule precise enough to be checked;
set up and organize a small self-access collection, physical or digital, to support contract work;
conduct short advising sessions that support learners without taking back control;
evaluate both the outcome of a contract and the learner’s management of the process;
recognize when a learner needs a more structured approach for a time, and adjust without blame;
state clearly which parts of a course are open to negotiation and which are fixed.

why: Why this matters. Tier II built autonomous capacity gradually. At C1, many learners are ready for a fuller, more formal structure that puts real direction-setting in their hands.

background.x: Henri Holec (1981: 3) defined autonomy as ‘the ability to take charge of one’s own learning’, and he spelled out what that involves: deciding objectives, content and progression, methods and techniques, monitoring the procedure, and evaluating what has been acquired. A learning contract is simply a document in which a learner makes each of those decisions explicit. The idea comes from adult education. Malcolm Knowles, whose theory of andragogy stressed that adults learn best when they help plan their own learning, developed contracts as a practical tool for self-directed study (Knowles 1975, 1986).

The key word is negotiated. David Little (1991) warns that autonomy is not the same as isolation or the absence of a teacher; it grows through interdependence and dialogue. Leni Dam (1995) showed that even school learners in Denmark could plan and evaluate their own work when the teacher handed over decisions gradually. Phil Benson (2011) summarizes a large body of research in the same direction: autonomy is best seen as a capacity that can be developed, and it develops unevenly, so support must be flexible.

In India the relevance is clear. NEP 2020 calls for flexibility in the choice of courses and for assessment that tracks each learner’s progress (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 describes the aim of developing learners who can learn independently (NCERT 2023). At the same time, most Indian learners have spent years in exam-driven, teacher-directed classrooms, and the fixed syllabus and board examination do not disappear. A realistic learning contract therefore works inside clear boundaries. It also treats the home language as a legitimate tool: a learner in Mysuru may plan in Kannada, keep a vocabulary log with Kannada glosses, or choose a Kannada novel in English translation as a bridge into extensive reading.

items: Contract quality. A signed contract with a goal, specific methods, named evidence and a criterion another person could check.
Process log. A dated log showing study sessions, adjustments and advising notes.
Two-part evaluation. A self-evaluation of outcome and process, supported by evidence.
Teacher portfolio. For teachers: a ‘fixed and free’ chart, two advising records and a short reflection on one learner who needed more structure.
Which decisions about learning do your learners currently make for themselves?
How do you respond when a learner’s goal differs from what you think they need?
What resources could you gather, at little or no cost, for a self-access corner?
In your advising, how often do you ask before you tell?
What is genuinely open to negotiation in your course, and what is not?

perm: All contracts, charts, teacher notes and dialogues are original and written for this book, and the learners named are fictional. Holec’s definition is quoted briefly with citation. Screenshots of Google Docs, Google Sites, Padlet or Canva require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Any real learner contracts or logs used in training need the learner’s consent.

terms.def: A professional practice in which an advisor helps learners reflect on and direct their own learning through dialogue, using techniques of listening, questioning and restating rather than instruction (Mynard and Carson 2012).
The theory and practice of teaching adults, which stresses that adults learn best when learning is relevant to their own goals and draws on their experience (Knowles 1980).
Mutual reliance between learners, or between learners and teachers. Autonomy grows through interdependence and dialogue rather than isolation (Little 1991).

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.

A written agreement, negotiated between learner and teacher, that sets out the learner’s goals, the activities and resources to be used, a timeline and how progress will be evaluated; a brief ‘mini’ version can be built into a single unit.

A learning goal agreed jointly by learner and teacher through discussion of the learner’s needs and interests, often recorded in a learning contract, rather than simply imposed by the teacher or syllabus.
Evaluation of how learning is progressing during a course or contract, rather than only at the end, so that goals and methods can be adjusted.

A room or space with organized learning materials, such as graded readers, audio, worksheets and answer keys, which learners use independently to work on their own goals, often with advice available (Gardner and Miller 1999).

Learning in which learners plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning, managing goals, strategies, motivation and time (Zimmerman 2000). Also called self-regulation, it is developed through goal-setting, self-monitoring and reflection.
